papers.title: MOLECULAR BASIS FOR PINK1 MATURATION
papers.summary: This paper investigates the molecular mechanism by which PINK1, a key mitochondrial kinase, undergoes maturation processing inside cells. PINK1 maturation involves its import into mitochondria and proteolytic cleavage steps that regulate its stability and activity. Understanding this process sheds light on how PINK1 is normally kept at low levels in healthy mitochondria versus stabilized on damaged ones to trigger mitophagy.
papers.why: PINK1 is the master initiator of mitophagy in neurons, so understanding its maturation mechanism is directly relevant to your studies of mitophagy/autophagy pathways in neuronal and interneuron populations.
papers.figure: Figure showing the proteolytic processing steps and structural determinants of PINK1 maturation (likely a schematic/structural figure of PINK1 cleavage sites).

papers.title: AMPK/mTOR/ULK1 signaling mediates ncoa4-dependent ferritinophagy in BPA-induced ferroptosis in HT-22 hippocampal neuronal cells.
papers.summary: This study investigates how bisphenol A (BPA), an environmental toxin, triggers a specific form of iron-related cell death called ferroptosis in HT-22 mouse hippocampal neuronal cells. The researchers show that this process depends on ferritinophagy, a selective autophagy pathway where the protein NCOA4 helps break down iron-storage ferritin, releasing free iron that drives oxidative damage. They demonstrate this ferritinophagy is controlled by the AMPK/mTOR/ULK1 signaling cascade, a well-known master regulator of autophagy initiation.
papers.why: This paper offers direct mechanistic insight into a selective autophagy pathway (NCOA4-mediated ferritinophagy) and its upstream AMPK/mTOR/ULK1 control in hippocampal neurons, relevant to understanding autophagy-linked neurodegeneration and iron dysregulation in the brain.
papers.figure: A figure showing autophagosome/ferritinophagy markers (e.g., NCOA4, LC3, ferritin colocalization) alongside AMPK/mTOR/ULK1 phosphorylation status under BPA treatment, ideally with pharmacological or genetic pathway inhibition.

papers.title: Redox-sensitive coordination of mitochondrial quality control: Integrating ROS, NAD<sup>+</sup>, and Ca<sup>2+</sup> signaling in disease.
papers.summary: This paper discusses how mitochondria maintain quality control through a coordinated network of signals involving reactive oxygen species (ROS), NAD+ levels, and calcium (Ca2+) signaling. It explains how imbalances in these redox and metabolic signals can disrupt mitochondrial health and contribute to disease. The review likely synthesizes molecular pathways linking mitochondrial stress sensing to broader cellular quality control mechanisms like mitophagy.
papers.why: Since mitophagy in neurons depends heavily on redox and calcium signaling that regulate mitochondrial quality control, this paper could provide key mechanistic insight relevant to understanding neuronal mitophagy dysfunction in the brain.
papers.figure: A schematic figure showing the integrated signaling network between ROS, NAD+, and Ca2+ in regulating mitochondrial quality control pathways.

papers.title: Targeting the 14-3-3θ protein with indole-3-propionic acid restores PINK1/Parkin mediated mitophagy and suppresses endothelial PANoptosis in atherosclerosis.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the metabolite indole-3-propionic acid affects blood vessel cells in atherosclerosis. It shows that this compound interacts with a protein called 14-3-3θ to restore a cellular cleanup process called mitophagy, which relies on the PINK1/Parkin pathway to remove damaged mitochondria. By restoring this process, the compound also blocks a harmful form of inflammatory cell death called PANoptosis in endothelial cells, potentially protecting against artery disease.
papers.why: Although focused on vascular endothelial cells rather than neurons, this paper offers mechanistic insight into PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy regulation, a core pathway directly relevant to studying mitophagy dysfunction in neurons and interneurons.
papers.figure: A figure showing the proposed mechanism linking 14-3-3θ, PINK1/Parkin mitophagy activation, and suppression of PANoptosis markers in endothelial cells.

papers.title: Selective quality control of mistargeted mitochondrial proteins at the endoplasmic reticulum
papers.summary: This paper investigates how cells handle mitochondrial proteins that fail to reach the mitochondria and instead accumulate at the endoplasmic reticulum. It describes a selective quality control mechanism that detects these mistargeted proteins and directs them for degradation or clearance at the ER. This helps prevent toxic protein buildup and preserves cellular protein homeostasis, particularly for mitochondria-destined proteins.
papers.why: Understanding how mistargeted mitochondrial proteins are cleared at the ER provides mechanistic insight into mitochondrial protein quality control pathways that intersect with mitophagy and autophagy regulation, which is central to the neuronal mitochondrial homeostasis studied in this PhD project.
papers.figure: A figure showing the pathway/mechanism by which mistargeted mitochondrial precursor proteins are recognized and degraded at the ER membrane.

papers.title: Nanotechnology for targeted modulation of mitophagy: molecular mechanisms, therapeutic applications, and translational perspectives.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how engineered nanoparticles and nanomaterials can be designed to specifically control mitophagy, the process by which cells clear damaged mitochondria. It covers the molecular pathways these nanotechnologies target, such as PINK1/Parkin and receptor-mediated mitophagy signaling. It also discusses potential clinical applications and the challenges of moving these nanotech approaches from lab research into real-world therapies.
papers.why: Since mitophagy dysfunction in neurons is central to your PhD work, understanding nanotechnology-based tools to precisely modulate mitophagy could inform future therapeutic strategies or experimental interventions relevant to interneuron and perineuronal net pathology.

papers.title: Connecting the dots: a centrosome-associated RAC1 signaling network links centrosome amplification with autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper explores how a signaling network centered on centrosomes, involving the protein RAC1, connects two cellular processes: centrosome amplification (having too many centrosomes) and autophagy (the cell's recycling system). The researchers mapped out how these centrosome-associated proteins interact with autophagy machinery. This suggests centrosomes may act as hubs that regulate whether cells degrade certain components via autophagy.
papers.why: While focused on cell division machinery rather than neurons directly, this paper's insights into autophagy regulation mechanisms could offer conceptual parallels or shared signaling components relevant to understanding mitophagy/autophagy pathways more broadly, even outside the centrosome context.

papers.title: IL17A disrupts autophagy-lysosomal function and lysosome reformation through the GSK3B-TFE3 signaling pathway in Huntington disease.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the immune signaling molecule IL17A disrupts autophagy and lysosomal function in the context of Huntington disease. The researchers identify a specific molecular pathway involving GSK3B and TFE3 proteins that mediates this disruption, particularly affecting the cell's ability to reform lysosomes after autophagy. The findings suggest IL17A signaling could be a therapeutic target for restoring proper autophagic-lysosomal function in Huntington disease.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it details a specific signaling pathway (GSK3B-TFE3 regulation of autophagy-lysosomal function) that could inform mechanistic understanding of mitophagy/autophagy dysregulation in neurodegenerative contexts, potentially applicable to interneuron vulnerability studies.
